<reason>Both sides were sharp, well-grounded, and format-compliant, but PRO built the cleaner path to victory. PRO's decisive live route was the capital-vs-operating cost gap: a carrier can sustain a completed network yet rationally refuse to build it, which means CON's voucher alternative either fails to solve supply gaps or becomes an expansion subsidy itself. CON's response—that thin take-up demand explains the refusal—was plausible but never fully neutralized, and CON's own closing retreated to "the connection may not justify its cost" in no-service areas, effectively conceding PRO's framework that subsidy is warranted where public value exceeds cost. PRO also landed two other strong responses: the "even when ≠ whenever they say so" reframe that blunted CON's trigger argument, and the symmetric-forecast point that "let technology close the gap" is itself a prediction CON never scrutinizes. CON's best material—the asymmetry between auditable carrier math and unauditable benefit projections, and the "discipline addresses fraud, not error" distinction—was genuinely strong and well-pressed via Q1, and PRO's appraisal answer (conservative valuations, published baselines, post-hoc evaluation) was adequate rather than decisive. CON also slightly overstated PRO's concession in the closing. Net: PRO answered more of the live pressure cleanly, while CON's core alternative had a hole it papered over. A close, high-quality debate won on the financing-gap clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B3.1/B4.4 press: if subscriptions cover operating costs but not construction, vouchers cannot secure a network without financing construction themselves—forcing CON into a concession that left PRO's core subsidy principle standing.</best_rebuttal>
